https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/crrv.text: Image caption, AnaÃ¯s de Vos suspects a cup of coffee that NÃ¨gre gave her was drugged By Nuala McGovern & Emma Ailes ,Â Reporting from Paris and Strasbourg Â and Â Amelia Butterly ,Â BBC World Service Published 7 hours ago "I was really weak. I couldn't really feel my legs any more," says AnaÃ¯s de Vos. "I was scared. I didn't know what was happening." It was July 2011 and AnaÃ¯s, who was then 27, was being interviewed for a job at France's Ministry of Culture in Paris. She didn't usually drink coffee but when the interviewer, a senior civil servant called Christian NÃ¨gre, offered her one, she agreed out of politeness. He made it himself, she tells BBC Global Women, but "it tasted badâ¦ so I drank about half". The meeting had started in the office, but after a few minutes NÃ¨gre suggested they go outside. As they strolled through Paris's streets, AnaÃ¯s began to feel an inexplicable and uncontrollable need to urinate. She says she told him she needed to find a toilet urgently. "He looked me right in the eye and said, 'Oh, do you need a wee?' "I felt like a child. I thought it was really weird the way he looked at me, almost gleeful." She says he directed her to the door of a storage cupboard under a bridge on the River Seine and said: "You can do it here." Now, AnaÃ¯s is one of nearly 250 women who believe NÃ¨gre drugged them in alleged incidents between 2009 and 2018, subjecting them to what is known as chemical submission, where drugs are used to gain control over someone. The concept of chemical submission came to prominence in France in 2024 when Gisele Pelicot's husband was found guilty of sedating her and inviting strangers to rape her while she was unconscious. Image source, Grand Est Region & Bas-Rhin Prefect Image caption, Nearly 250 women accuse NÃ¨gre of drugging them between 2009 and 2018 "I started to panic," AnaÃ¯s continues. "I had visions of him pushing me into the room and closing the door behind me." Feeling it was "too strange", she insisted they move on. They walked to the Louvre to use the toilets there, but they cost one euro and she had left her purse at the ministry's offices. NÃ¨gre told her he didn't have any cash either. Desperate and in pain from trying not to urinate, AnaÃ¯s found a cafe that let her use their toilet. By then, "I felt really weak physically", she says. As she approached the bathroom, she lost control and wet herself. Accused: France's mass drugging case Women who accuse a civil servant of drugging them at job interviews share their stories Watch on iPlayer Viewers outside the UK can watch on YouTube Thinking back to 2011, AnaÃ¯s gets some comfort from the fact that when she did urinate, it was out of NÃ¨gre's sight. "At least he didn't see me," she says. "I was so grateful I was only wearing a dress," she adds, explaining it made it easier to disguise what had happened. After three hours with NÃ¨gre, she says she "felt dizzy and drained". She didn't get the job and had suspicions about him, but could never work out exactly what it was that had made her feel so uncomfortable. AnaÃ¯s felt the incident damaged her self-confidence and in the years that followed, she ended up on a less ambitious career path. Image source, Mohammed Badra/EPA/Shutterstock Image caption, AnaÃ¯s directed them to the Louvre in the hope of using public facilities there Then in 2019, she received a letter from the police. When she met them, she learned they suspected she was one of almost 200 women NÃ¨gre was accused of drugging during job interviews, purportedly for roles at the ministry. "I was shocked," she says. "But I was happy to know I wasn't crazy. Something had happened that day." Dozens more alleged victims have since emerged. Police believed NÃ¨gre had used diuretics, which are used to manage a number of medical conditions, including high blood pressure, and cause the body to produce excess urine. AnaÃ¯s had had a fleeting thought the day she had met NÃ¨gre, that maybe he had slipped something into her drink, but put it aside telling herself: "It's the Ministry of Culture. It's not possible." 'Experiments P' AnaÃ¯s says police told her they found a spreadsheet of the alleged victims on NÃ¨gre's computer, entitled Experiments P, which was how they found her. The document, she says, noted the time the women arrived for their interviews, when the diuretic was administered, how long it took before they urinated, and what underwear they were wearing. Looking back, AnaÃ¯s is now convinced the strange taste in the coffee NÃ¨gre made her was the diuretic. The investigation into NÃ¨gre began in June 2018, when he was caught by a colleague taking a photograph of a woman from beneath a table, the prosecutor's office said in a statement released in February this year. He was initially suspended from his job as regional director of cultural affairs before being sacked by the Ministry of Culture in 2019. Prosecutors said that in 2018 he told investigators he had "imposed humiliating situations on women" during job interviews. Many of the women say the first time they realised they may have been victims was when police contacted them. Some came forward when they saw AnaÃ¯s and other accusers in media reports. NÃ¨gre, who is in his 60s, is now under formal investigation on charges that include drugging, invasion of privacy and sexual assault. He is awaiting trial. The BBC put the allegations contained in this article to NÃ¨gre through his lawyer, but he declined to comment. Figure caption, "I had tears streaming down my cheeks from pain," Marie-HÃ©lÃ¨ne Brice tells BBC Another person named in NÃ¨gre's notes was Marie-HÃ©lÃ¨ne Brice. He interviewed her for a job at the Ministry of Culture in 2016 in Strasbourg, where he was then working. She says he told her she looked stressed and suggested they take a walk outside to "calm her nerves". But as they strolled along the canal, Marie-HÃ©lÃ¨ne, like AnaÃ¯s, felt an uncontrollable need to urinate, which began to cause her pain. She says NÃ¨gre told her that he knew of a public toilet nearby, but when they arrived at the location there was no toilet. "I was really starting to sufferâ¦ pains to the point that I was white, pale, I had tears streaming down," she says. Marie-HÃ©lÃ¨ne says she had no choice but to urinate in public. She says NÃ¨gre offered to shield her with his jacket. "I was terribly embarrassed," she says. "He didn't take his eyes off me." Marie-HÃ©lÃ¨ne says that for years she felt ashamed. Like AnaÃ¯s, she was also contacted by police who told her she was among NÃ¨gre's alleged victims. "It was a very big shock," she adds. Chemical submission Marie-HÃ©lÃ¨ne says that as well as psychological distress, she has also been left with urinary problems. She explains that while the events might not fit the pattern of what people usually think of in cases of sexual assault, she has no doubts about what happened to her: "I have been attacked, I have been intoxicated, I have been poisoned, but for me it is a sexual assault, clearly." The issue of chemical submission has been picked up by French MP Sandrine Josso. She became a leading campaigner after French senator Joel Guerriau was found guilty this year of spiking her drink with ecstasy in order to sexually assault her. Josso argues that for too long France has not done enough to support women who have been drugged and prosecute offenders. Image caption, French MP Sandrine Josso has become a leading campaigner on the issue of chemical submission She was behind the introduction this year of a pilot programme where women who suspect they have been drugged can take samples of blood, urine or hair to a lab for testing, without having to file a formal complaint with police. "People are mobilising, victims are reporting more, filing more complaints, and that's important," Josso tells BBC Global Women. But there are limitations. AnaÃ¯s, Marie-HÃ©lÃ¨ne and many other alleged victims of NÃ¨gre did not suspect they had been drugged - and unless testing takes place very soon after drugging, substances won't show up in blood and urine samples. Drugs may be detectable for longer in hair, but as time passes it becomes harder to pinpoint when they were administered. The use of diuretics in this way is "very unusual" according to Prof Jean-Claude Alvarez, who runs the pilot at the Raymond-PoincarÃ© AP-HP Hospital. He says he has never seen anything like it in 26 years as a toxicologist. Image caption, Prof Jean-Claude Alvarez tests samples, including hair, for drugs in the toxicology lab The lab routinely tests for 400 substances and "now, in France, we are looking for diuretics", he adds. It is now 15 years since AnaÃ¯s's encounter with NÃ¨gre and seven years since she first spoke to police. Like many of the other accusers, she is frustrated at the length of time it is taking for NÃ¨gre's case to come to court. Meanwhile, the alleged perpetrator has continued to work in human resources, according to Fondation des Femmes, a women's rights group that is supporting about 30 of the women affected. "Everything is unsettling and I am angry at how we are treated," says AnaÃ¯s, who is now 42 years old. She says she first spoke to police in 2019, but then heard nothing about the case until 2023, despite emailing them many times. "For four years, I was alone with the knowledge that I was a victim. I didn't know what to do," she says. "I am very angry with the justice system." Marie-HÃ©lÃ¨ne describes this waiting as "secondary victimisation". "As a victim, I have to prove the impact, go to a psychiatrist, write specific notes," she says. The delays to the case have made what happened harder to bear. "We do not necessarily feel [we are] completely taken seriously," Marie-HÃ©lÃ¨ne says. Kalliopi Mingeirou from UN Women told the BBC that governments, police and justice systems needed to do more to tackle drug-facilitated sexual assault, and that authorities were facing "very serious challenges" and delays in cases of alleged abuse are "destroying women's lives". The BBC asked the French police, judiciary and government to respond to the criticisms of their handling of the case, but they did not respond. For a long time, Marie-HÃ©lÃ¨ne was silent until she stopped feeling shame. "I don't have to hide myself - I am a victim," she says. "It is important for me to speak publicly because it allowed some victims to recognise themselves, to discover they were a victim and to file a complaint in turn. "Speaking out is necessary in the world in which we live, it is important to talk about sexist and sexual violence." Photograph: Ritchie B Tongo/EPA Nvidia Nvidia hires leading US law firm to investigate Jensen Huang’s relationship Move comes as chipmaker reels from reports its CEO was having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy Business live – latest updates Dan Milmo and Graeme Wearden Wed 11 Nov 2026 06.49 EST Last modified on Wed 11 Nov 2026 07.08 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Nvidia has appointed a leading US law firm to conduct a “thorough and independent” investigation into the relationship between its chief executive, Jensen Huang, and an alleged Chinese spy . The $4.1tn (£3tn) chipmaker has hired New York-based Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz for the investigation, which will be led by the Wachtell partner Joon Kim. Wachtell’s website describes Kim, a former government prosecutor in New York, as a specialist in areas including internal investigations, white-collar criminal and regulatory defence, and crisis management. Nvidia did not give a timeframe for the investigation but the company has said Huang will continue to lead the business he co-founded “without interruption”. The company is reeling from an espionage scandal after reports that its chief executive had been having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang, who was also an Nvidia customer. The US ambassador to China , David Perdue, said: “The situation with Nvidia is another reminder that we have to stay diligent. “National security is part of this economic conversation because economic security is national security. And so, what we’re doing with China is bumpy right now,” he told Bloomberg Television. Nvidia had at first denied an improper relationship with the Chinese citizen, who is no relation to the Nvidia boss, but Huang then admitted on Sunday he had been unfaithful to his wife – without referring directly to Ms Huang. On the same day Nvidia announced an investigation into reports that Huang “has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort”. The scandal has wiped $430bn off Nvidia’s value as shareholders gauge the potential impact of the scandal on a company and an executive who are synonymous with the AI boom. Wachtell is one of the most prestigious corporate law firms in the US. Its founding partner Martin Lipton invented the “poison pill defence” in the 1980s, a corporate gambit that helps companies ward off hostile takeovers. Technically called the “shareholder rights plan”, the poison pill allowed investors to buy more shares at a discount if one shareholder acquired a certain percentage of the company’s stock. This made it harder for corporate raiders to acquire a company without the board’s approval. The firm was closely involved in the takeover of Getty Oil by Texaco. This was the largest corporate takeover in history at the time, although it turned sour when the thwarted suitor Pennzoil sued Texaco and won. In 2008, a team of Wachtell lawyers advised the US Treasury department on the takeover of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac during the financial crisis. The company was founded in the 1960s and is said to be the most profitable law firm in the US. It pulled in revenues of $5.1m per lawyer last year and made profits of $12m per partner, the highest profits per partner ever, according to the Am Law 100 rankings . From 2017 to 2018, Kim was the acting US attorney for the southern district of New York, where he ran a team of lawyers investigating securities and commodities fraud, mail and wire fraud, public and private corruption, money laundering, cybercrime, and tax offences. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning after newsletter promotion That included the case of the former US representative Anthony Weiner , who was sentenced to 21 months in prison for sending obscene material to a minor. He also oversaw the prosecution of the banker Mehmet Hakan Atilla, who was convicted in 2017 of helping to evade US sanctions on Iran . Another high-profile assignment landed on Kim’s desk in 2021, when he investigated multiple allegations of sexual harassment by the then New York governor, Andrew Cuomo. One analyst has put Huang’s chances of leaving Nvidia at 15%. “Right now the Street and investor chatter is assigning roughly a 15% chance he is removed as CEO of Nvidia with a high probability (85%) he stays on as CEO after the board investigation is completed,” wrote the tech analyst Dan Ives in a note to investors. “We would expect a board investigation that could take four weeks to six weeks and will create a clear overhang on the stock until more news emerges from Nvidia.” Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, the senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management and the founder of the Chief Executive Leadership Institute, has put Huang’s survival chances at “about 50-50”.
